title: Baraka and the Warm Blanket
summary: It’s getting hotter on Shosho’s farm, and Baraka wants to know why. Kinyonga, a chameleon who turns orange when he’s too hot, takes him high above the clouds to see the warm blanket of air around our Earth, and what we can do to keep it just right.
learn: Why Kenya gets droughts and floods
How trees and clean energy help
cover_alt: Cover of Baraka and the Warm Blanket: Baraka, his grandmother Shosho and Kinyonga the chameleon in a dry maize field.
pages: Baraka and the Warm Blanket. By Dunia Endelevu.

The sun shone brightly over Machakos, turning the dusty earth a pale, warm brown. Nine-year-old Baraka sat under an acacia tree, fanning himself with his favorite sketchbook. Nearby, his grandmother, Shosho, inspected the curled leaves of her maize field. “The afternoon is so heavy with heat today,” Baraka sighed. Shosho wiped her forehead and smiled gently. “When I was a little girl, the rains came like clockwork every season,” she said. “Now, the heat feels stronger, and the rains are uncertain.”

Suddenly, a tiny movement caught Baraka’s eye on the wooden fence. A small chameleon slowly shifted from a shade of bright green to a warm, vibrant orange. “Phew!” a cheerful voice squeaked. “I’m Kinyonga, and I turn orange when it gets too hot!” Baraka gasped in delight. Kinyonga swiveled one giant eye towards the sky. “Do you know why today is so hot? Today’s heat is the weather—what the sky is doing right now. But climate is the usual pattern of weather over many, many years.”

Before Baraka could ask another question, Kinyonga’s curly tail wrapped gently around Baraka’s wrist. In a flash of magical imagination, the tail uncoiled into a giant, sparkling ribbon that lifted them high above the clouds! Up, up, up they soared into space. Looking back, Baraka saw planet Earth gleaming blue and green, surrounded by a delicate layer of air. “Look closely,” Kinyonga said, pointing his tiny nose. “Earth wears a thin, glowing blanket made of invisible gases.”

Kinyonga clapped his tiny front feet together. “This invisible blanket traps just enough joto—that’s warmth from the sun—to keep our planet cozy,” he explained. “Without this blanket, Earth would be far too cold for humans, maize plants, or chameleons to live! It keeps the temperature just right for all living things.” Baraka marveled at the gentle glow wrapping around the big blue world below them.

But as they floated closer to the ground, Kinyonga’s expression became serious. Far below, cars, busy factories, and big power plants were puffing out soft grey clouds of gas into the air. “When people burn coal, oil, and gas, it adds extra carbon dioxide into the air,” Kinyonga explained softly. “And when large forests are cut down, there are fewer trees to soak up that extra gas.”

Baraka watched as the grey puffs floated up into the atmosphere, making the blanket around Earth grow thicker and thicker. “A thicker blanket traps far too much joto,” Kinyonga said. “Did you know our whole planet is now more than one degree Celsius warmer than it was 150 years ago? That sounds like a small number, but for an entire world, it’s a huge change!”

With a gentle whoosh, the imagination journey landed Baraka back on solid ground. Now he understood what Kinyonga meant. In Kenya, a warmer planet causes longer dry spells that make Shosho’s soil dry and cracked. At other times, it brings heavy downpours that cause floods over distant roads, making it hard for children to travel safely.

“Is there hope?” Baraka asked, looking down at his sketchbook. Kinyonga puffed out his chest proudly. “Of course! Look at Kenya!” Kinyonga pointed toward the Rift Valley, where giant plumes of clean white steam rose high into the air. “This is geothermal energy! Deep underground heat makes steam, which creates clean electricity without making the blanket thicker. Most of Kenya’s electricity comes from clean sources like this!”

The next day at school, Baraka put his learning into action. He joined his friends in the school garden to plant fresh young trees. “Trees are natural superheroes,” Baraka reminded his classmates. “They absorb carbon dioxide from the air!” Before leaving the classroom later, Baraka remembered to click off a light switch in the empty hallway, knowing that saving energy helps keep the air clean.

That evening back at the farm, Baraka showed Shosho a colorful drawing in his sketchbook. It showed Earth wrapped in a healthy, perfectly warm blanket, surrounded by green trees and bright sunshine. Nearby on the fence, Kinyonga rested peacefully, his skin back to a brilliant green under the gentle shade. Shosho hugged Baraka warmly. “You are learning how to care for our home,” she smiled. Today, switch off one light you are not using, and tell someone why!

title: Kobe and the Web of Life
summary: There are no bees in the school garden, and Amani wants to know why. Kobe, a wise old leopard tortoise, shows her and Otieno the glowing web that joins every living thing, then flies them over Kenya’s wild places to see why each thread matters.
learn: How living things depend on each other
Why bees and other pollinators matter
cover_alt: Cover of Kobe and the Web of Life: Amani and Otieno kneel beside Kobe, a leopard tortoise, in a dry school garden.
pages: Kobe and the Web of Life. By Dunia Endelevu.

The school garden was quiet and mostly dry. Seven-year-old Amani knelt by a dusty flowerpot. “Look, Otieno,” she whispered softly, pointing to a small yellow blossom. “There are no bees today.” Otieno leaned down to see. Nearby, under a low bush, something moved very slowly. It was a big leopard tortoise! “Hello,” said the creature in a gentle voice. “My name is Kobe.”

Kobe blinked his kind, wrinkly eyes. He had lived in the garden for many, many years. “Do you know what biodiversity is?” Kobe asked gently. Amani shook her head. “Biodiversity means all the different kinds of living things on Earth—plants, animals, insects, tiny microbes, and the places where they live. We are all part of one big, wonderful family.”

Kobe slowly extended a claw and drew a circle in the dry dirt. Magically, bright glowing lines began to sparkle in the soil! The light connected pictures of a fuzzy bee, a flower, a juicy mango, a small bird, a seed, and a tall tree. “Living things depend on each other, just like threads in a web,” Kobe explained. “When one thread breaks, others are affected.”

“Bees and other pollinators carry pollen from flower to flower,” Kobe said. “This helps plants make fruits and seeds, such as delicious mangoes and avocados.” Amani smiled as she imagined plump fruits hanging from leafy branches. Nearby, Otieno touched his tummy as it gave a loud rumble. “I love mangoes!” he cheered.

Suddenly, Kobe’s shell began to glow. In their imagination, his shell grew into a giant flying boat! Whoosh! Amani and Otieno soared high into the sky. Below them, tall giraffes nibbled acacia leaves on the sunny savannah. Soon, they glided into the lush green msitu—the famous Kakamega Forest—where monkeys swung through thick trees and colourful birds sang.

Next, the magic shell flew over Lake Nakuru, where thousands of pink flamingos splashed in the water. Then they zoomed all the way to the bright coral reef at Watamu on the coast! Looking down through the clear waves, they saw colorful fish swimming and a sea turtle gliding by. Otieno cheered out loud, “Kenya has so many amazing wild places!”

But then, the glowing web showed a sadder picture. Gently, the children saw what harms the web: a cut-down forest, plastic rubbish in a river, and dry, hot land caused by climate change. A few of the glowing threads snapped and faded away. “When wild places are harmed, the web of life grows weaker,” Kobe said softly.

Amani touched her hearing aid and thought carefully. “We can fix the threads!” she exclaimed. They ran to find their teacher. Smiling warmly, their teacher clapped her hands. “What a wonderful idea!” she said. Together, the class gathered small spades to plant native indigenous trees and a bright patch of flowers for the bees.

Weeks later, the school garden buzzed with busy bees, butterflies, and singing birds. Their teacher gathered the class together in the shade. “Did you know Kenya plans to grow 15 billion trees by 2032?” she shared proudly. “Planting indigenous trees and flowers gives animals and insects food and homes. Every single tree counts!”
Amani bent down low and spotted a tiny red ladybird resting on a leaf. Under the shade of a new bush, Kobe smiled his slow, wise smile. The web of life was glowing strong once more.

title: Is It Fair, Babu?
summary: When another class uses up all the water in the school tank, Wanjiru cries, “That is just not fair!” Her grandfather Babu helps her see that the air around our Earth is shared in the same way, and why climate change hurts most the people who did least to cause it.
learn: Who caused climate change, and who is hurt most
How to share fairly and save rainwater
cover_alt: Cover of Is It Fair, Babu?: Wanjiru in her school uniform smiles up at her grandfather Babu outside a school with a water tank.
pages: Is It Fair, Babu? By Dunia Endelevu.

At break time, Wanjiru’s class ran eagerly to the school water tank. But when they turned the tap, only a weak trickle came out—and then stopped completely! Another class had used almost all the water before them. Wanjiru’s friends sighed in disappointment, feeling hot and thirsty under the afternoon sun. Wanjiru looked at the empty metal tank and frowned. “That is just not fair!” she exclaimed.

That evening, Wanjiru sat on the veranda with her grandfather. Babu listened carefully as she told him about the water tank. He smiled gently and stroked his beard. “You have just understood something very big, Wanjiru,” Babu said softly. “The air around our Earth is shared by everyone, just like one big water tank shared by a whole school. When someone takes too much or pollutes it, everyone feels the impact.”

A letter arrived from her pen pal, Hassan, who lived far away in northern Kenya. Wanjiru opened the envelope and pictured his village in Marsabit. It had not rained there for a very long time. In her mind, she saw Hassan walking across the dry earth alongside his father, searching for fresh water for their family’s goats and camels under a blazing sun.

Back in the living room, Babu slowly spun an old globe. “For many, many years,” Babu explained, “big busy cities far across the ocean built factories, drove millions of cars, and ran huge power stations. They burned coal, oil, and gas, puffing grey clouds into the sky. Those countries that burned the most fuel caused most of climate change.”

Babu pointed to the continent on the globe. “Look here,” he said quietly. “Over Africa, there is only a tiny puff by comparison. Africa produces only about 4 out of every 100 parts of the world’s greenhouse gases.” Wanjiru stared at the map, thinking deeply. It felt so unfair that a region contributing so little to the pollution was impacted so heavily.

Yet in Hassan’s home in Marsabit, families faced severe droughts. In another town, heavy rain caused riverbanks to overflow. Wanjiru felt a surge of hope as she pictured neighbors working together during the flood, carrying belongings to higher ground and helping each other stay safe.

Wanjiru pictured a grand hall where adults made big decisions about the planet. But in her mind, the chairs around the table were far too tall for children, and no one was listening to young voices. Children did the least to cause climate change, but they will live with it the longest, and they are rarely asked what they think.

Babu nodded gently as Wanjiru shared her thoughts. “This is why we talk about haki,” Babu said. In Kiswahili, haki means fairness and justice. “Climate justice means that those who caused more pollution must do more to cut it and help others get ready. It means protecting those most at risk—and ensuring everyone, including children, gets a say.” In Wanjiru’s mind, a grown-up pulled up child-sized chairs to the table.

The next morning at school, Wanjiru knew just what to do. Her class created a fair schedule for the water tank so every grade got a turn, and together they set up gutters to collect rainwater. At assembly, Wanjiru spoke bravely about haki. Afterwards, she sat down to write back to Hassan to tell him everything she had learned.
During break time, the two school classes gathered by the rainwater collector. They shared cups of fresh water and laughed together under the shade of a wide tree. The water was shared fairly now.

title: The Little Steps Club
summary: Kip thinks children are too small to do anything about something as big as climate change. Leila points to a weaver bird building its nest one blade of grass at a time, and starts a club to show how little steps add up to something huge.
learn: The two parts of climate action
Little ways to save energy, water and waste
How a school can get ready for hot, dry days
cover_alt: Cover of The Little Steps Club: Leila, in her yellow wheelchair, and Kip look up at a weaver bird in an acacia tree.
pages: The Little Steps Club. By Dunia Endelevu.

At break time, Leila sits in her bright yellow wheelchair under the shade of an acacia tree. Up above, a bright yellow weaver bird works busily on a branch. Kip runs across the yard in his red running shoes and flops down on the bench. “We’re just kids, Leila,” Kip sighs, wiping his forehead. “How can we do anything about something as big as climate change?”

Leila points up at the tiny yellow bird holding a long strand of grass in its beak. “Look at the weaver bird,” Leila says gently. “It doesn’t build a whole nest in one second. It carries one blade of grass at a time. Loop by loop, strand by strand. Soon, the whole tree is full of nests!” Kip looks up, a big grin spreading across his face. “So lots of small steps add up to something huge?” “Exactly,” Leila smiles.

Leila starts ‘The Little Steps Club’! Kip, twin sisters Achieng and Awino, and their teacher Mr Mwangi gather around a chalkboard. Mr Mwangi adjusts his glasses and taps the board. “Climate action has two main parts,” he explains. “First, cutting the pollution that warms our planet—like saving energy and planting trees. Second, getting ready for changes—like saving rainwater for dry times and staying safe in hot weather!”

The club members start taking little steps at home. Kip switches off unused lights and turns off the TV when leaving the room. At their home, twins Achieng and Awino stand together at the sink. “Turn off the tap while brushing!” says Achieng. “…to save every drop!” finishes Awino. Meanwhile, Leila sits at her table carefully gluing the wheel back onto a broken toy bus instead of throwing it away.

On Saturday, Kip goes to the market with his father. Instead of asking for plastic bags, Kip carries a sturdy woven reed basket filled with vegetables. Mr Mwangi walks past holding a fabric tote bag and waves. “Did you know?” Mr Mwangi says, “Kenya banned plastic carrier bags back in 2017 to keep our environment clean!”

At school, the club starts a tree nursery! Mr Mwangi helps lay a smooth, wide dirt path so Leila’s wheelchair can easily roll alongside the garden beds. Leila uses a small trowel to scoop rich earth into pots, while Kip carries a light watering can over to help.

Next to the garden, the club digs a compost pit for lunch leftovers and fruit peels, turning food waste into rich soil. They also attach a rain collection barrel under the school roof drainpipe. “When the dry season comes,” Achieng says, “we’ll have stored rainwater…” “…so our little trees won’t go thirsty!” adds Awino.

To get ready for weather changes, the twins create an Early Warning Board near the school gate. Every morning, they check the sky and temperature. On very hot days, they hold up a bright painted sign at morning assembly. “Drink extra water today!” calls Achieng. “And rest in the shade!” shouts Awino.

Soon, the whole school wants to join in! At assembly, Mr Mwangi steps up to speak. “In 2015, almost every country in the world signed the Paris Agreement, agreeing to work together to slow down global warming,” Mr Mwangi says. “When we work as one, in Kiswahili we say pamoja!” The entire school cheers, “Pamoja!”

Months later, the schoolyard is shaded by growing young trees. Up in an acacia branch, the yellow weaver bird weaves its final blade of grass into a perfect, round nest. Leila, Kip, Achieng, Awino, and Mr Mwangi rest under the breezy leaves, proud of what they built together step by step. Choose one little step for this week, and ask a friend to do it with you!
